turns.text:
## A Minor — Classical Version

Your draft progression is solid. I'd make one small adjustment: use E7 instead of E in bar 2 for the stronger dominant pull, and end with a clear perfect cadence.

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Am | **Bar 2:** E7 | **Bar 3:** F | **Bar 4:** E7 → Am

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – E – G – A – G – E – G – A
**Bar 2:** G# – B – E – G# – B – G# – E – D
**Bar 3:** C – F – A – C – A – F – E – D
**Bar 4:** E – G# – B – E | A – C – E – A (half bar E7, half bar Am)

### Left Hand (block chords or broken, quarter notes)
**Bar 1:** A₂ – C₃ – E₃ (root position, two hits or held)
**Bar 2:** E₂ – G#₂ – B₂ – D₃ (E7, root position)
**Bar 3:** F₂ – A₂ – C₃ (root position)
**Bar 4:** E₂ – G#₂ – B₂ on beat 1, then A₂ – C₃ – E₃ on beat 3

### Voice-Leading Tips
Keep common tones between chords stationary. Am to E7: the E stays, C moves down a half step to B, A moves down to G#. E7 to F: G# resolves up to A, B moves up to C, D moves up or stays depending on voicing. This gives you smooth stepwise motion almost everywhere, which is the hallmark of classical voice leading. Avoid jumping all three voices at once.

---

## A Minor — Modern/Sparse Version

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Am (open fifth, no third) | **Bar 2:** Am/E (pedal E in bass) | **Bar 3:** F add9 (no third) | **Bar 4:** Am (open fifth)

### Right Hand (melody, same rhythm)
**Bar 1:** C – E – G – A – G – E – G – A
**Bar 2:** same motif or slight variation: C – E – G – A – B – A – G – E
**Bar 3:** C – F – G – A – G – F – E – D
**Bar 4:** C – E – G – A – G – E – D – A (land on A, hold)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** A₂ and E₃ (open fifth, held whole note)
**Bar 2:** E₂ (single bass pedal, whole note)
**Bar 3:** F₂ and C₃ (open fifth), or F₂ – G₂ – C₃ for the add9 color
**Bar 4:** A₂ and E₃ (return to open fifth, whole note)

The left hand here is deliberately still. Let the right hand do all the movement. The emptiness of open fifths leaves the major/minor quality ambiguous, which is the modern sound you're after.

---

## C Minor — Classical Version

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Cm | **Bar 2:** G7 | **Bar 3:** Ab | **Bar 4:** G7 → Cm

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – G – Ab
**Bar 2:** G – B – D – G – F – D – B – D
**Bar 3:** C – Eb – Ab – C – Ab – Eb – D – C
**Bar 4:** B – D – G – B | C – Eb – G – C (half bar G7, half bar Cm)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** C₂ – Eb₂ – G₂ (root position)
**Bar 2:** G₂ – B₂ – D₃ – F₃ (G7, root position)
**Bar 3:** Ab₂ – C₃ – Eb₃ (root position)
**Bar 4:** G₂ – B₂ – D₃ on beat 1, then C₂ – Eb₂ – G₂ on beat 3

### Voice-Leading Tips
Cm to G7: Eb moves down a half step to D, G stays, C moves down to B. G7 to Ab: B resolves up to C, D moves up to Eb, F moves up to Ab or down to Eb. The leading tone (B natural) should always resolve upward to C — this is the most important voice-leading rule in minor-key classical harmony.

---

## C Minor — Modern/Sparse Version

Your draft progression works well. I'd refine it slightly.

### Progression
**Bar 1:** Cm (open fifth) | **Bar 2:** Cm/G (G pedal) | **Bar 3:** Ab (open fifth) | **Bar 4:** Cm over Bb pedal

### Right Hand (melody, eighth notes)
**Bar 1:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – G – Ab
**Bar 2:** C – Eb – G – Ab – G – Eb – D – C
**Bar 3:** Ab – C – Eb – Ab – G – Eb – D – C
**Bar 4:** C – Eb – G – C – Bb – G – Eb – C (descend to final C, hold)

### Left Hand
**Bar 1:** C₂ and G₂ (open fifth, whole note)
**Bar 2:** G₁ (single bass pedal, whole note — the low G gives depth)
**Bar 3:** Ab₁ and Eb₂ (open fifth, whole note)
**Bar 4:** Bb₁ (pedal, whole note — the Bb creates tension under the Cm melody that resolves when the melody lands on C)

### Voice-Leading Tips for the Modern Versions
Voice leading in sparse textures is about bass motion. Move the bass by step or by third rather than by fifth — that keeps the modern, floating quality. C pedal to G pedal (down a fourth or up a fifth) is the biggest leap here, and it works because it's a pedal tone shift rather than a chord change. The Ab to Bb bass motion at the end is stepwise, which feels natural and inevitable.

---

## General Practice Suggestion
Play through the classical versions first to internalize the harmonic gravity, then play the modern versions and notice how the same melody feels different over open voicings. That contrast will teach you a lot about how harmony shapes the character of a line.

### Bar 1: Am
**RH (8ths):** C4 – E4 – G4 – A4 – G4 – E4 – G4 – A4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 3 – 4
**LH (quarters):** [A2–C3–E3] on beats 1, 2, 3, 4 (hold or re-strike gently)
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1

### Bar 2: E7
**RH (8ths):** G#4 – B4 – E5 – G#4 – B4 – G#4 – E4 – D4
**Fingering:** 2 – 3 – 5 – 2 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1
**LH (quarters):** [E2–G#2–B2–D3] on beats 1 and 3, rest or sustain on 2 and 4
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 2 – 1

### Bar 3: F
**RH (8ths):** C4 – F4 – A4 – C5 – A4 – F4 – E4 – D4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1
**LH (quarters):** [F2–A2–C3] on beats 1, 2, 3, 4
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1

### Bar 4: E7 → Am
**RH (8ths):** E4 – G#4 – B4 – E5 (beats 1–2) | A4 – C5 – E5 – A4 (beats 3–4, land on A4 and hold)
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 | 1 – 2 – 3 – 1
**LH:** [E2–G#2–B2] on beat 1, [E2–G#2–D3] on beat 2, [A2–C3–E3] on beat 3 (hold through beat 4)

## C Minor Classical — Andante, mp

### Bar 1: Cm
**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 – G4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 3 – 4
**LH (quarters):** [C3–Eb3–G3] on beats 1, 2, 3, 4
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1

### Bar 2: G7
**RH (8ths):** G4 – B4 – D5 – G4 – F4 – D4 – B3 – D4
**Fingering:** 1 – 3 – 5 – 1 – 1 – 5 – 3 – 5
**LH (quarters):** [G2–B2–D3–F3] on beats 1 and 3, sustain on 2 and 4
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 2 – 1

### Bar 3: Ab
**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – Ab4 – C5 – Ab4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1
**LH (quarters):** [Ab2–C3–Eb3] on beats 1, 2, 3, 4
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1

### Bar 4: G7 → Cm
**RH (8ths):** B3 – D4 – G4 – B4 (beats 1–2) | C4 – Eb4 – G4 – C5 (beats 3–4, hold final C5)
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 | 1 – 2 – 3 – 5
**LH:** [G2–B2–D3] on beat 1, [G2–B2–F3] on beat 2, [C3–Eb3–G3] on beat 3 (hold through beat 4)
**Fingering:** 5–3–1 shifting to 5–3–1

---

## Playability Notes

The left hand stays in a narrow range (roughly A2 to G3) so you rarely need to move your hand position. The only real shift is in bar 4 of each sketch, where you move from the dominant chord to the tonic on beat 3 — practice that transition slowly until the hand finds the new position by feel.

For the right hand, the thumb (finger 1) acts as the pivot point. When the melody descends at the end of bars 2 and 3, let the thumb take over early so you're set up for the next bar.

Use a light sustain pedal, changing on each new chord. In the modern versions you wrote earlier, you could hold the pedal longer for wash, but in these classical sketches, clean changes keep the voice leading audible.

## C Minor Modern — Andante, p

### Bar 1: Cm (no 3rd)
**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 – G4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 3 – 4
**LH:** [C3–G3] open fifth, whole note
**Fingering:** 5 – 1
*(Alternative: [C2–C3–G3] octave plus fifth, fingering 5–2–1, adds weight)*

### Bar 2: Cm/G (G pedal)
**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 – G4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1
**LH:** G2 single bass pedal, whole note
**Fingering:** 5 alone
*(Alternative: [G2–D3] open fifth, fingering 5–1, slightly brighter)*

### Bar 3: Ab (no 3rd)
**RH (8ths):** Ab3 – C4 – Eb4 – Ab4 – G4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 1
**LH:** [Ab2–Eb3] open fifth, whole note
**Fingering:** 5 – 1
*(Alternative: [Ab2–Bb2–Eb3] with added 9th, fingering 5–4–1, mirrors the Fadd9 color from the A minor version)*

### Bar 4: Cm/Bb (Bb pedal)
**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – C5 – Bb4 – G4 – Eb4 – C4 (hold final C4 as quarter)
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 4 – 3 – 2 – 1
**LH:** Bb1 single bass pedal, whole note
**Fingering:** 5 alone
*(Alternative: [Bb1–F2] open fifth, fingering 5–1, the low Bb against the C melody creates a beautiful unresolved tension — let it ring)*

---

## Playability Notes

The left hand barely moves in these sketches, which is intentional. The modern sound comes from stillness in the bass against a moving melody. Resist the urge to fill in more notes.

Pedaling is different here than in the classical versions. Hold the sustain pedal through entire bars, or even across bars 1 and 2, to let the overtones blend. The open fifths won't muddy the way full triads would, so longer pedal creates atmosphere rather than mess.

Dynamics should stay around p to mp throughout. If you want a slight arc, crescendo gently into bar 3 and pull back in bar 4. The final held note in each version should decay naturally — lift your hands but keep the pedal down and let it fade.

The voicing alternatives in parentheses are mix-and-match. Try bar 1 with the octave-plus-fifth alternative and bar 4 with the simple open fifth for contrast, or the reverse. The point is to find the amount of space that feels right to you.

## The Transition Fingering Tip

The hardest moment is the shift from bar 2 into bar 3, where your left hand goes from a single pedal tone or open fifth to full triads on every beat. Here is how to make it smooth: during the last two eighths of bar 2, while the right hand is still playing, silently move your left hand into position over the bar 3 chord. Your left hand has nothing to do on those last two eighths since it is sustaining a whole note, so use that time to hover over F–A–C (A minor version) or Ab–C–Eb (C minor version). The pedal release at the end of bar 2 gives you a tiny breath of silence that disguises the texture change, so the shift from floating to grounded feels like an arrival rather than a jolt.

---

## Why the Hybrid Works

The open fifths in bars 1–2 leave the harmony suspended and ambiguous. When bar 3 introduces the full triad and bar 4 delivers the dominant-to-tonic cadence, the resolution feels earned precisely because you withheld it. The listener hears two bars of atmosphere and then two bars of direction, and the contrast between stillness and motion is what gives the sketch its shape.

**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 4 – 5 – 4 – 3 – 2
**LH:** E2 single pedal tone, whole note
**Fingering:** 5 alone
**Pedal:** hold from bar 1, release on last eighth of bar 2

### Bar 3: F — broken arpeggio
**RH (8ths):** C4 – F4 – A4 – C5 – A4 – F4 – E4 – D4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1
**LH (quarters, broken arpeggio pattern: bottom–middle–top–middle):**
Beat 1: F2 / Beat 2: A2 / Beat 3: C3 / Beat 4: A2
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1 – 3
**Pedal:** fresh pedal on beat 1, hold through bar (the broken notes are all from one chord so they won't clash)

### Bar 4: E7 → Am — broken arpeggio into cadence
**RH (8ths):** E4 – G#4 – B4 – D5 (beats 1–2) | C4 – E4 – A3 – A3 (beats 3–4, land on A3 and hold)
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 | 2 – 3 – 1 – 1
**LH (quarters):**
Beat 1: E2 / Beat 2: G#2 / Beat 3: A2 / Beat 4: E3
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 4 – 1
**Pedal:** change pedal on beat 1, change again on beat 3 with the Am arrival, hold to end

### Fingering Tip
In bar 2 your left hand sits on E2 with finger 5 doing nothing for four beats. On the last eighth, slide your thumb to hover over A2 while keeping finger 5 near F2. When bar 3 arrives, finger 5 drops to F2 and you're already in position for the ascending arpeggio. The distance from E2 to F2 is a single half step, so the shift is almost invisible.

**RH (8ths):** C4 – Eb4 – Ab4 – C5 – Ab4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 3 – 5 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1

Beat 1: Ab2 / Beat 2: C3 / Beat 3: Eb3 / Beat 4: C3
**Fingering:** 5 – 3 – 1 – 3

**RH (8ths):** B3 – D4 – G4 – F4 (beats 1–2) | Eb4 – C4 – C4 – C4 (beats 3–4, settle on C4 and hold)
**Fingering:** 1 – 2 – 4 – 3 | 2 – 1 – 1 – 1

### Fingering Tip
Bar 2 has your left hand on G2 with finger 5. Bar 3 starts on Ab2 with finger 5. That is one half step up, even easier than the A minor version. During the last eighth of bar 2, let your hand float up that half step so finger 5 rests on Ab2. The arpeggio pattern in bar 3 is identical in shape to the A minor version (bottom–middle–top–middle), so once you've learned one you've learned both.

---

## Why Broken Arpeggios Work Here

The block chords in the earlier classical version created a clear textural break between the sparse bars and the functional bars. The broken arpeggios soften that border. Your left hand goes from stillness (whole note) to gentle motion (quarter-note arpeggio) rather than from stillness to sudden chordal weight, so the shift from atmospheric to functional feels like waking up gradually rather than flipping a switch. The harmonic information is identical — same chords, same cadence — but the delivery is smoother.
